records.question: What journal entries does each party book in a tokenized trade?
records.answer: The entries follow the economic object, not the technology. At each step only the parties whose own books hold the cash, the security or the claim debit or credit anything; a token, a chain or a software provider books nothing by itself. The cards below print every entry, step by step.

records.question: When a crypto firm collapsed, did its customers get their money back, and how?
records.answer: Rarely in full. Of 10 cases the library tracks, customers are being paid back, at least partly, in 3 (Cryptopia liquidation, Mt. Gox civil rehabilitation, FTX Chapter 11 distribution), no payout is confirmed in the library's record for 5, and 1 recovered everything (Wuhan virtual-currency cash-out fraud). How much comes back depends on whether a court treats customer crypto as the customers' own property held in trust or as the failed firm's assets.

records.question: Which countries license stablecoins, and what must back them?
records.answer: The library tracks 22 jurisdictions. Each card says who must license a stablecoin issuer there, what has to back the coin and what holders can claim, and which issuers are actually operating.

records.question: Which licensed stablecoins outside the U.S. are actually live, and is their backing proven?
records.answer: The library tracks 13 stablecoin products outside the U.S. 6 are live under a local license, and 4 of those publish regular attestations of their reserves (USDG · Singapore; XSGD · Singapore; XUSD · Singapore; Zand AED / AEDZ · United Arab Emirates). The rest are in beta, announced, used without a local license, or have no dated public proof of backing yet; the backing of 1 failed.

records.question: Which crypto networks and companies would the Fed's stablecoin rules reach, and how?
records.answer: The Federal Reserve Board's two GENIUS Act proposals of September 24, 2026 reach the 20 crypto networks and companies the library maps in four different ways: 2 would face them directly as stablecoin issuers (Ripple / XRPL and Circle / USDC / CPN / Arc / Tazapay); 4 as custody, distribution or payout services (Securitize, Cash legs & tokenized bank money, Coinbase / Base / Tokenize and SWIFT ledger & bank obligations); 12 as technical systems an issuer would run on; and 2 sit outside the direct issuer rules (Bitcoin and DTC / DTCC tokenization). The proposals are not final, and they approve no company, network or token.

records.question: Which tracked crypto dollars are excluded, likely outside, unresolved or wound down?
records.answer: Of these 19 saved entries, six are deposits or securities excluded by the Act’s text; eight are assessed by the Library as likely outside the definition, without a regulator ruling; three remain unresolved or issuer-dependent; and two are wound down. Each card keeps its own evidence date.

records.question: When can an investment adviser hold clients' crypto keys itself under the SEC proposal?
records.answer: Only as a last resort, and only if the proposal becomes final; the SEC proposed it on October 1, 2026 and no final rule has been issued. For an ordinary advisory client the rule reaches a crypto asset only when it is a fund or security. The adviser may hold the keys itself only when, after a written inquiry, no qualified custodian will hold that particular asset (cost does not count), re-checked at least quarterly, and it must move the asset to a custodian as soon as reasonably practicable once one is available. Only designated supervised people may hold key material, every movement needs at least two of them including a management person, and a technology vendor must not be able to reach the keys or move the assets alone, so a single-employee adviser cannot use the route.

records.question: Which states have made gold money or put bitcoin in a state reserve, and when does each take effect?
records.answer: Gold, yes; bitcoin, not as money. Florida's gold-and-silver legal-tender law took effect July 1, 2026; in Texas, the law makes gold and silver specie legal tender from September 1, 2026, and the state's electronic gold currency may start no sooner than May 1, 2027. Louisiana (June 11, 2025, with a gold-payment registry added June 23, 2026) and Missouri (July 10, 2025) signed gold legal-tender laws whose start dates are not in the record. For bitcoin the rows show reserves, not money: New Hampshire and Arizona passed reserve laws in May 2025, Texas made the first state purchase on November 20, 2025, and Wisconsin's pension sold its stake. Every row is a reconstructed summary without an official link.

records.question: Where does the CLARITY market-structure bill stand, draft by draft?
records.answer: It is not law. The CLARITY Act (H.R. 3633) passed the House, and Senate sponsors released three public drafts: EHF26654 (616 pages, July 22, 2026), EHF26718 (630 pages, September 10, 2026) and EHF26724 (635 pages, September 14, 2026). None was formally filed as an amendment. On September 15, 2026 the Senate voted 49 to 50 on taking the bill up, short of the 60 votes needed, and the library's web check on October 19, 2026 found no later step.

records.question: What in Genesis is actually built and running, and what is still planned?
records.answer: Of the 12 saved Genesis project profiles, 2 have a demonstrated workflow or partly operating services (OPAL and American Science Cloud/ModCon). NNSA has 1 authorized cloud environment, with Genesis workload deployment unproved. Another 4 are being built or designed, 4 are selected or planned, and 1 is consortium membership. The separate proposed Argonne center remains market research without a solicitation or award.
